content: Testing for common or highly fatal infections must be carefully balanced against the urgency of transplanting a viable organ. Corneal transplantation, which is frequently performed in developing countries, should not proceed without first ruling out the possibility that the deceased donor may have died from rabies. Concentrated, purified cell culture and embryonated egg-based rabies vaccines (CCEEs), developed over four decades ago, have been proven safe and effective for both pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). These vaccines, administered to millions globally, are highly effective when combined with proper wound management and simultaneous administration of rabies immunoglobulins after exposure, even in high-risk cases. WHO strongly recommends discontinuing the use of nerve tissue vaccines due to their severe adverse reactions and lower immunogenicity compared to CCEEs. Currently, nerve tissue vaccines are produced for human use only in Algeria, Argentina, Bolivia, and Ethiopia, and their replacement with modern CCEEs is strongly advised. CCEEs are produced by propagating the rabies virus in cell substrates such as human diploid cells, Vero cells, primary chick or duck embryo cells, or embryonated duck eggs. After growth, the viral harvest is concentrated, purified, inactivated, and lyophilized. These vaccines are not supplied in multidose vials for intramuscular or intradermal injection and do not contain preservatives like thiomersal. They have a shelf life of at least three years when stored at 2–8°C and protected from sunlight. Once reconstituted with sterile diluent, the vaccines should be used immediately or within six hours if kept at 2–8°C, as partially used vials may become contaminated. WHO prequalification ensures the quality, safety, and efficacy of vaccines for use in national immunization programs, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Prequalification involves a review of the production process, quality control procedures, and consistency of vaccine lots, as well as audits of manufacturing facilities. Vaccines must meet international standards of quality and good manufacturing practices. Three rabies vaccines are currently prequalified for intramuscular use: purified Vero cell rabies vaccine, purified chick embryo cell vaccine, and purified duck embryo vaccine. Intradermal administration of rabies vaccines is promoted by WHO as a safe, immunogenic, and cost-effective alternative to intramuscular administration. This method reduces vaccine volume and direct costs by 60–80% compared to standard intramuscular injection. Intradermal vaccination provides an equivalent immune response at a lower dose, making it a vaccine-sparing option for both PrEP and PEP. Proper training is essential to ensure full intradermal instillation of the vaccine and to avoid accidental subcutaneous injection. Opened vials should be stored at 2–8°C for no longer than 6–8 hours. Scheduling follow-up PrEP visits within similar periods can help minimize vaccine wastage. Vaccine manufacturers should provide clinical evidence that new products are immunogenic, effective, and safe when administered intradermally and include suitability for intradermal vaccination on the product label. Clinical trials for rabies vaccines should evaluate their use for PrEP and PEP with various vaccination schedules and routes of administration, as well as the onset, extent, and duration of protection. Trials should adhere to WHO guidelines for good clinical practice and be approved by relevant national regulatory authorities.
